1.title: your grandmother before dinner
1.hook: your grandmother before dinner; a gift you didn't earn
1.howItsDone: Many Catholic families say a short grace before meals, often the traditional "Bless us, O Lord," and many make the sign of the cross before and after it.

segments.voice: Picture a kitchen table. The food is on it, steam coming off the potatoes, and somebody's already reaching for the bread. And then a hand on the wrist. Your grandmother, or someone's grandmother, saying: wait. Grace first. Heads go down. A few quick words, a quick amen, and then everybody eats. Millions of families have done this every night of their lives, and most kids at that table thought grace meant the little speech before dinner. It does. But the word is much bigger than the speech. It's the reason for the speech. Today's word is the first one on this path, and in a sense every other word sits on top of it.
screen: `A KITCHEN TABLE.` → `WAIT. GRACE FIRST.` → `THE WORD IS BIGGER THAN THE SPEECH.`

segments.voice: Grace comes from the Latin word gratia. It means a favor. A gift. Something given freely, not paid for. It's the same root that gives English the word gratitude, and the word gratis, meaning free of charge. The New Testament was written in Greek, and there the word is charis, which also means a gift freely given, and a kind of loveliness. So when Catholics talk about grace, they mean God's gift of himself, given before anybody earned it. The letter to the Ephesians says it plainly, in the old Douay-Rheims Bible that English-speaking Catholics used for centuries: "For by grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God." Not of yourselves. That's the surprise at the heart of the word. You don't climb up to grace. It comes down to you. Catholics say it arrives in many ways: in baptism, in the sacraments, in prayer, in an ordinary Tuesday when a friend calls at exactly the right moment. And here's where the dinner table comes back in. The old grace many Catholic families say goes like this: "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen." Listen to what it notices. Thy gifts. Thy bounty. The food on the table is a small picture of the big thing. Somebody grew it, somebody cooked it, and before any of that, Catholics say, somebody gave the world to begin with. So saying grace isn't paying a fee before eating. It's noticing that you were given something. That's the whole shape of today's word: a gift you didn't earn, and the moment you notice it.
screen: `GRATIA — A FAVOR, A GIFT.` · `CHARIS — GIVEN FREELY.` · `NOT OF YOURSELVES.` · `THE TABLE IS A SMALL PICTURE.` · then, large: `A GIFT YOU DIDN'T EARN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for day one, and it's small on purpose. One breath, with the bell. Before you breathe, think of one thing you have today that you didn't earn. The air, maybe. A person. A roof. Then breathe in slowly, all the way, and let it out. If you pray, you can say thank you with that breath. If you don't, just let yourself notice the gift.
Grace. A favor, a gift freely given. Catholics say it comes first, before anyone earns it. First word on your strand.
screen: `GRACE — your 1st word` → clicks onto an empty word-strand.

segments.voice: Your line to carry: you are already held. Grace means the gift came first. Today, before one meal, even a snack at your desk, pause for a single second and notice that it was given to you. That's day one. See you tomorrow.

2.title: the smallest prayer
2.hook: the smallest prayer; what the hand is tracing
2.carry: head, heart, shoulders — all of you
2.tomorrow: why people stand up when the book comes in
2.howItsDone: Catholics make the sign of the cross at the start and end of prayers and of the Mass, often after dipping their fingers in holy water on entering a church, touching forehead, chest, left shoulder and right shoulder.

segments.voice: Yesterday, grace: a gift you didn't earn, noticed at a kitchen table. Your line was: you are already held. Did you catch yourself noticing a gift? Day two.

You've seen it even if you've never done it. A soccer player jogging onto the field, touching forehead, chest, one shoulder, the other. A grandmother passing a church on the bus. A pitcher before the first throw. Someone hearing bad news in a hospital hallway. It takes about two seconds, and nobody has to say a word out loud. It's so quick that people forget it's a prayer at all. It might be the smallest prayer there is, and it's how most Catholic prayers begin and end, including the grace from yesterday. Today, what the hand is actually tracing.
screen: `FOREHEAD, CHEST, SHOULDER, SHOULDER.` → `TWO SECONDS.` → `THE SMALLEST PRAYER.`

segments.voice: It's very old. Around the year 200, a Christian writer in North Africa named Tertullian described believers tracing a small cross on their foreheads all day long: when they got dressed, when they sat down to eat, when they lit a lamp. A tiny mark with a thumb. Over the centuries the small cross grew into the large one most Catholics make today. And the hand tells a story as it goes. It traces the cross, the shape Jesus died on, over your own body. At the same time, the words name who Catholics believe God is. They come from the end of Matthew's Gospel, where Jesus sends his friends out, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." So in two seconds you've said two big things: the cross, and the Trinity, one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Catholics say it's also a small reminder of their own baptism. That's why, walking into a church, many dip their fingers in holy water first, and then make the sign. Now look at where the hand goes. The forehead, where you think. The chest, where your heart is. Then both shoulders, where you carry things and do your work. Many Catholics hear it that way: the prayer covers all of you. Your thoughts, your feelings, your strength. A small detail you might notice at a friend's church: Catholics in the West usually go to the left shoulder first, then the right. Orthodox Christians go right, then left, and hold their fingers a particular way. Same sign, two old habits.
screen: `TERTULLIAN: A THUMB ON THE FOREHEAD.` · `THE CROSS AND THE TRINITY.` · `A REMINDER OF BAPTISM.` · `THINK, FEEL, CARRY.` · then, large: `ALL OF YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. One breath, with the bell. If you'd like to, make the sign of the cross slowly, slower than anyone ever does it: forehead, chest, left shoulder, right. If you'd rather not, just rest a hand on your forehead, then on your chest, then on each shoulder, and notice each place. Then one breath, all the way in and all the way out.
The sign of the cross. The cross traced over your own body, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Second word.
screen: `THE SIGN OF THE CROSS — your 2nd word`.

segments.voice: Your line: head, heart, shoulders — all of you. Today, when you catch yourself thinking, feeling or carrying something heavy, notice which of the three it is. Day two.

screen: `DAY 2 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY PEOPLE STAND UP WHEN THE BOOK COMES IN.`

3.title: why people stand up when the book comes in
3.hook: why people stand up when the book comes in
3.howItsDone: At Mass, Catholics sit for the first readings and the psalm, then stand for the Gospel, often tracing small crosses on the forehead, lips and heart as it is announced.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sign of the cross: forehead, chest, one shoulder, the other. Your line was: head, heart, shoulders — all of you. Which one was carrying the most? Day three.

If you've ever been to a Catholic Mass as a guest, you know the feeling. Everyone else seems to know when to sit, when to stand, when to kneel, and you're half a second behind, watching the person in front of you. There's one moment that catches visitors most. People have been sitting quietly, listening to readings. Then music starts, often the word alleluia, and the whole room stands up at once. Someone at the front lifts a book up high. Why stand for a book? For the next three days we're going to walk through the Mass like a play in three scenes. Today, scene one: the story.
screen: `SIT, STAND, KNEEL.` → `THE WHOLE ROOM STANDS.` → `SCENE ONE: THE STORY.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Mass comes from the old Latin ending of the service, ite, missa est, roughly: go, you are sent. So the whole thing is named for the moment you walk back out the door. Now, scene one. Catholics call it the Liturgy of the Word, and it's mostly listening. On a Sunday there's usually a reading from the Old Testament, then a psalm, often sung back and forth, then a reading from one of the letters of the apostles. People sit for those. Then comes the Gospel, one of the four books about the life of Jesus, and everyone stands. Catholics say that when the Gospel is read, Christ himself is speaking to the people gathered there. So you stand the way you'd stand when someone important walks into the room. There's a small ritual right before it, too. Many people trace three little crosses with their thumb: on the forehead, on the lips, on the heart. Remember yesterday's sign? It's the same idea, shrunk down. The words be in my mind, on my lips, in my heart. Standing for the book isn't new, either. The Bible itself describes it. In the book of Nehemiah, after the exile, the scribe Ezra opens the book of the law in front of the whole people, and when he opens it, they all stand up. And in Luke's Gospel, when Jesus goes home to Nazareth, he goes to the synagogue and stands up to read the scroll of Isaiah. People have been rising for the reading for a very long time. Then everyone sits again, and a priest or deacon preaches: the homily. The story has entered the room, and scene one ends.
screen: `MASS — GO, YOU ARE SENT.` · `READINGS, A PSALM, THEN THE GOSPEL.` · `THREE SMALL CROSSES.` · `EZRA OPENS THE BOOK. THEY STAND.` · then, large: `THE STORY ENTERS THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Three breaths, with the bell. If you're sitting, stand up, just for this, the way the room stands for the Gospel. On the first breath, touch your forehead. On the second, your lips. On the third, your heart. You don't have to say anything. Just let each place get ready to listen.
The Mass, scene one. The Liturgy of the Word: readings, a psalm, and the Gospel, which everyone stands to hear. Third word.
Your line: the story enters the room. Today, when someone starts telling you something that matters to them, give it the full attention of a room standing up. Day three.
